name: PT Adhi Kartiko Pratama Tbk

frontmatter.title: Adhi Kartiko Pratama — a reserve-limited ore price taker priced close to fair
frontmatter.summary: NICE sells low-grade nickel ore into Indonesian RKEF smelters at the government HPM price. We move to HOLD: the reserve-limited life DCF sits below the share price, but the probability-weighted value and a normalised EV/EBITDA cross-check are not, and the two errors offset. The rating rests on the life and the nickel price, not on a liquidity discount.
thesis: NICE is a price taker, not a price maker — its ore is sold on the ESDM HPM schedule, so the equity is a leveraged bet on a government-set ore price, not on LME nickel directly.

Volume now follows the company's own plan; the life is set by the only reserve evidence in the record, the regulator's statement that national nickel reserves support less than ten years of production.
The mine depletes inside the model — two tapered years carry the reserve to zero and there is no terminal value, so the wind-down is priced rather than assumed away.

The controlling shareholder is LX International via PT Energi Battery Indonesia, with ITMG at 9.62%; free float is 10.4%, below the exchange minimum — a liquidity and index risk, not an operating one.

On our numbers the equity is worth roughly what it trades at; the case for owning it is a reserve statement, an HPM grade upgrade or a strategic buyer, and all three are in the scenarios, not the base.

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Adhi Kartiko Pratama Tbk (NICE) at **HOLD** with a twelve-month target of **Rp229**, -2.3% against the Rp234 close. The company is a nickel-ore miner in North Konawe, Southeast Sulawesi, controlled since its 2024 listing by LX International of Korea through PT Energi Battery Indonesia [S6], with PT Indo Tambangraya Megah holding a 9.62% stake bought at Rp438 a share in July 2025 [S4][F9].

The target is built in three steps and a reader should hold them apart. The reserve-limited life DCF values the shares today at **Rp140**, below the Rp234 price; rolled forward twelve months at the cost of equity it is Rp159. Probability-weighting the bear, base and bull cases takes it to Rp254 — above the price, because a nickel upcycle and a reserve extension are worth a great deal to an asset with this much operating leverage, and the bear case is not a fall but a wipe-out. The house liquidity discount of 10.0% for a 10.4% float then gives **Rp229**. So the target is not the discounted DCF: it is a probability-weighted value that the discount brings back to the share price, and the rating is a statement that the market is roughly right, not that the life DCF's lower number is the answer.

The investment question is narrow. NICE does not sell nickel metal; it sells laterite ore to RKEF smelters at a price set by the government's Harga Patokan Mineral schedule, and its margin is the gap between that administered price and its own mining, hauling and barging cost [S13]. Everything that matters therefore reduces to four numbers: how many wet tonnes it sells, what grade the ore carries (the HPM table steps from US$25.3/wmt in the lower grade band to US$45.8/wmt one band up [S13][F5][F6]), what the royalty take is, and how long the orebody lasts. Our model is built on exactly those four, calibrated on the last actual year.

Our variant view is not that the company is badly run — the volume record is good, from 2,010 kt wmt in 2023 [S2][F1] to a 2,500 kt plan for 2025 and 2026 [S2][F3], and Q1 2024 sales grew by a third year on year to 350.8 kt wmt [S5][F13]. The variant view is narrower than the one we published at initiation: the ore body is reserve-limited, the company's own plan is the base, and at those two facts the equity is worth about what it costs. Our reserve-limited DCF values the shares at Rp140; the probability-weighted, twelve-month target is Rp229. To justify today's price the DCF needs a nickel price of 19,610 — above both the house deck's through-cycle marker and spot [S9][F7] — before any allowance for a longer life.

Three things move the value. First, **grade and realisation**: our realised ore price is 0.18% of LME nickel per tonne, calibrated on the actual revenue; a one-band upgrade in the HPM schedule roughly doubles revenue per tonne and is worth more than any volume assumption in this report. Second, **life**: the model depletes an opening FY2025A reserve of 25,000 kt of ore — nine years at the plan rate, then a 2,000 kt taper year and a 500 kt residual year — and carries nothing after it; a company reserve statement replaces that construction and the bull case tests a life half as long again. Third, **the funding path**: capex of IDR238.6bn in FY2025A left free cash flow to the firm at IDR-132.6bn and took gross debt to IDR236.8bn by 31 March 2026 [S0], but on the last actual's working-capital ratio FY2026E funds itself and net debt falls to IDR126.3bn.

What we are explicitly not doing: we are not taking a haircut to the ore price below the government schedule, we are not assuming volume declines inside the plan window, and we are not marking the mine life down to a number we cannot source. The base case is the most probable path at the deck's through-cycle nickel; the bear is a nickel trough plus a shorter reserve, the bull a tighter Indonesian ore market plus a published reserve.

NICE is a single-asset nickel-ore producer. Its mine sits at Lameruru village in North Konawe regency, Southeast Sulawesi, close to the coast and reachable from Kendari [S3], and the company has operated since 2008 [S3]. It ships laterite ore to smelters — the product is a smelter feedstock, not a metal — and the company states that the overwhelming majority of its revenue comes from nickel-ore sales [S10]. The profile also lists port, industrial-estate and laboratory-testing services [S3][S0]; those are ancillary to the mine and are not separately disclosed, so this model carries no other-revenue line.

The share register is the most important part of the business description. PT Adhi Kartiko Pratama listed on IDX in January 2024, offering about a fifth of its enlarged capital to the public at an indicative range set in the prospectus [S10][S6], and was immediately acquired by LX International Corp through PT Energi Battery Indonesia, an entity 99.99% owned by LXI, under a conditional sale and purchase agreement signed in November 2023 [S6][F11]. The stated strategic logic was access to Korea's electric-vehicle ecosystem and downstream processing [S10]. In July 2025 ITMG bought a 9.62% stake at Rp438 a share [S4][F9][F10], which put a second Indonesian resources group on the register alongside the Korean parent. Insiders and controlling holders own 89.6% of the shares and free float is 10.4% [S0] — a float below the exchange's minimum threshold, which shapes both the liquidity discount in our valuation and the stock's behaviour around news.

Operations are simple to describe and hard to differentiate. The company mines, hauls and barges ore; it does not smelt, so it captures none of the nickel-unit margin an RKEF or HPAL operator earns and carries none of a smelter's capital intensity. Volume history is short but consistent: 2,010 kt wmt produced in 2023 [S2][F1], a 1,800 kt target for 2024 [S2][F2] with 350.8 kt sold in Q1 2024 [S5][F13], and guidance of 2,500 kt for both 2025 and 2026 [S2][F3]. In Q1 2024 the company grew volume by a third while sales value fell by a quarter, to IDR136.3bn [S5][F14] — the whole business model in one sentence: it can grow tonnes and still shrink rupiah revenue when the ore price falls.

The board and management are Korean-led following the acquisition: Chang Pyo Hong as President Director, with a supervisory board chaired by Hyek Seo Koo and an audit committee chaired by an independent commissioner [S5]. A director resigned in June 2025, disclosed to the exchange with the company stating it had no operational or financial impact [S5]; the market marked the stock down around that disclosure during a period of operating-profit pressure [S5]. Employee count is 877 [S0], which is consistent with a contractor-heavy open-pit operation rather than an integrated industrial group.

Indonesian nickel ore mining is structurally a contractor business: the operator holds the IUP licence
and the mine plan, while overburden removal, hauling and barging are typically outsourced, which keeps
headcount low and makes the cash cost per tonne sensitive to diesel and to the haul distance to the
coast. Laterite deposits are shallow and mined in benches, with limonite (lower grade, higher moisture)
over saprolite (higher grade, feed for rotary-kiln electric furnaces). The grade split matters more than
the tonnage, because the government price schedule prices nickel units, not tonnes.

Indonesia is the marginal supplier of nickel ore to the world and the price-setter for the feedstock NICE sells. The policy lever is the RKAB, the annual work-and-budget approval that caps how much each miner may produce. For 2026 the ministry approved a national nickel quota of about 290 Mt, higher than the range initially planned [S8][F8], and the Director General has said the 2027 quota will be set with the LME and Shanghai surplus in mind — a surplus he described in the hundreds of thousands of tonnes [S8]. That is the single most important industry fact for this name: the regulator is explicitly managing the ore price, and it chose a larger quota for 2026 than it first intended.

The price NICE receives is administered. ESDM publishes a monthly Harga Mineral Acuan and derives the Harga Patokan Mineral by grade; the formula was re-set by a ministerial decision in April 2026, which adjusted the nickel-ore Corrective Factor, added iron, cobalt and chromium by-product credits and moved the quotation from a dry to a wet tonne basis — the ministry said the change was made precisely because Indonesian ore prices were too low and a market premium was not being captured [S14]. For the second half of October 2026 the schedule steps from US$25.3/wmt in the limonite band to US$45.8/wmt one grade band up and US$59.1/wmt two bands up [S13][F4][F5][F6]. The step between the limonite band and the next one is not a smooth gradient — it is a grade cliff — and it is why the most valuable piece of information about this company would be the grade of the ore it actually ships, which the archived record does not give us. Spot ore prices were falling through late October as RKEF lines shut and smelter stockpiles covered roughly two months of consumption [S13].

The metal price has been firmer than the ore price. LME three-month nickel rose to US$16,375/t in early November 2026, a five-week high, after Indonesia tightened enforcement of ore-trading rules [S9][F7]. That is a supply-enforcement rally in the ore market, not a demand recovery, and it sits on top of a market the regulator itself describes as oversupplied [S8]. The house metals deck carries a through-cycle marker of US$17,500/t, above the US$16,375/t spot [S9][F7], which is the price we use for value. The macro desk's stance on Indonesian supply-discipline names in nickel is favourable, and this report carries that tilt in the bull case rather than in the base.

Competitive position is weak by construction. NICE is a small ore supplier in a province with dozens of similar operations; it has no pricing power (the HPM sets the price), no product differentiation (ore is ore), no downstream integration (it sells to smelters it does not own), and no reserve disclosure that would let it claim a long-life position. Its advantages are locational — close to the coast and to Kendari [S3] — and relational: a Korean parent with an EV-battery interest and an Indonesian coal group on the register are useful for offtake and for funding. Against that, the cost-curve position is unknown: no archived source gives NICE's cash cost per tonne in a peer-comparable form, so we cannot place it in a quartile. What we can say is that its reported margin is thin relative to the ore price it receives, which implies a mid-curve position at best.

Five forces, briefly. **Supplier power** is moderate: contractors and fuel set a large part of the cost base, and the fuel link is in the model [S13]. **Buyer power** is high: a handful of RKEF smelters buy ore in a province where the quota is larger than the smelters' appetite, and the price they pay is anchored to a government schedule they helped negotiate. **New entrants** are constrained by the RKAB and by the 2026-2027 policy tightening, the one genuinely supportive force. **Substitutes** are limited near term — nickel pig iron and matte both need ore — but Indonesian ore competes with Philippine and New Caledonian supply at the margin. **Rivalry** is high: many small miners, one administered price, and a regulator actively managing volumes.

Regulation cuts both ways. The upside is enforcement: tighter policing of ore-trading activity is what lifted the metal price in early November [S9]. The downside is that the same ministry sets the quota, and its stated aim is to keep enough ore flowing to domestic smelters [S8]. For a price taker, that is a ceiling on pricing power dressed as industrial policy.

**History.** Revenue ran IDR867.8bn in FY2022A, IDR927.9bn in FY2023A, fell to IDR616.0bn in FY2024A and rebounded to IDR1,177.7bn in FY2025A [S0]. The shape follows the ore price, not the tonnage: Q1 2024 is the clean example, with volumes up a third and sales value down a quarter [S5][F13][F14]. Gross margin went from 20.2% in FY2022A to 16.6% in FY2024A and 22.4% in FY2025A [S0]. The reported net result in FY2025A was a loss of IDR-26.7bn despite the best revenue year in the record, and the reason is a fourth-quarter charge: Q4 2025 EBIT was a large loss against a solid profit in Q3 on a similar revenue base [S0]. That is a one-off of that scale sitting inside operating expenses, which took FY2025A opex to IDR226.5bn against IDR48.3bn a year earlier [S0]. We treat it as non-operating and do not forecast it; a reader should know that reported EBITDA of IDR42.9bn understates the underlying run-rate by approximately that amount.

**Revenue build.** Our model sells ore, not nickel: volume in kt of wet tonnes, multiplied by an ore price per wmt, converted at the macro deck's rupiah path. Base volume is 2,500 kt, the company's own plan for 2025 and 2026 [S2][F3], held flat through FY2034E and then stepped down as the reserve runs out. The previous draft ran 2,500 kt on a second crusher; no archived source describes that crusher or any capacity figure, so it is now a bull-case assumption rather than part of the plan the report describes. Revenue is IDR1,351.2bn in FY2026E and IDR1,445.1bn in FY2027E, with IDR1,484.4bn at the plateau.

The realised price is the number that needs the most defence. We calibrate it on FY2025A: revenue of IDR1,177.7bn over the volume the plan implies gives a realisation of 0.18% of the LME metal price per tonne. The cross-check is the government schedule — the limonite HPM of US$25.3/wmt against an LME of US$16,375/t is a ratio a shade lower than ours [S13][F5][F7] — so our ratio sits between the weaker grade band and the stronger one, which is where a company selling a blended laterite product should sit. We hold it flat across the forecast. We do not take a haircut to the HPM and we do not assume a grade upgrade.

**Costs.** Cash cost is built from mining at US$12.0 per wmt, hauling, barging and port at US$5.5 per wmt, plus the royalty line and a fuel escalation tied to the coal deck's ici4 series. That combination reproduces FY2025A reported cost of sales of IDR914.1bn to within a few percent [S0], the test we set ourselves. Cost is held flat in nominal dollars and escalated only through fuel — no real-term deflation without a source, and no strip-ratio creep without a mine plan, as the method card requires. Royalty is the weak point: we could not archive NICE's effective nickel-ore royalty, so the model carries the engine constant of 13.5% and flags it. If the true take is closer to the statutory nickel-ore schedule, EBITDA is understated by a visible amount every year, and this is the assumption we would most want an LK note for. The one policy fact we can source points the other way: ESDM has postponed the mineral royalty increase it had consulted on, so no step-up is modelled [S16]. At IDR182.4bn against EBITDA of IDR242.2bn the line is the single largest call on the margin after the ore price itself, which is why we flag it rather than bury it.

**Cash flow, capex and debt.** Capex was IDR238.6bn in FY2025A against IDR116.7bn in FY2024A, and free cash flow to the firm was IDR-132.6bn [S0]: the company has been building, and gross debt went from IDR52.0bn to IDR133.8bn and then to IDR236.8bn at the latest balance sheet [S0] — a bank facility plus working-capital lines, booked in FY2026E as net new borrowing so that the model's debt line agrees with the balance sheet the market sees. Equity was IDR147.9bn at FY2025A [S0]. Gross debt at the 31 March 2026 balance sheet is IDR236.8bn [S0]; net debt at that date is struck before the FY2026E operating cash flow and so stands above our FY2026E forecast net debt of IDR126.3bn, which is 0.5 times FY2026E EBITDA and a different picture from the 2.9 times that the reported FY2025A EBITDA produces — the difference is entirely the fourth-quarter charge discussed above, not a change in the debt. That is the balance-sheet risk in the name: leverage measured on a normalised year is comfortable, and leverage measured on the year the accounts actually printed is not, which is why we carry no dividend and no new borrowing after FY2026E.

Working capital is negative and structural: the company funds itself on supplier credit, with IDR-186.9bn of operating working capital against revenue of IDR1,177.7bn [S0], and current liabilities exceed current assets by a multiple at the same date [S0]. Negative working capital flatters cash conversion in a growth year and reverses in a contraction, which is worth remembering when the volume profile turns down after FY2028E.

**Earnings-quality flags.** We ran the house screen on the data that exists, which is four years of the pack's receivables, inventory and payables series rather than none. *Accruals*: FY2025A net loss against positive operating cash flow gives a strongly negative accruals ratio — but that positive cash flow rests on a large working-capital release, so the honest reading is that cash ran ahead of earnings only because supplier credit grew, and on operating cash flow before that release the company was roughly break-even. *Divergence*: inventory grew more than two and a half times while cost of sales rose by about four fifths, and it was not written down, which is the one divergence flag the screen raises [S0]. Receivables did not outgrow revenue over the same period, and the FY2024 fall in receivables with revenue is consistent rather than suspicious [S0]. *The Q4-2025 charge*: we could not identify it from an announcement — the two announcement pages in the registry carry no item text — and it sits in operating expenses in the same quarter that current liabilities jumped by an amount of the same order [S0]. We therefore keep it out of the forecast as non-operating, state that this is a judgement and not a sourced treatment, and note that if it is a provision or a tax true-up rather than an impairment it is a cash obligation that would come off the equity value directly. *IDX regime*: no special-monitoring board or notation flag appears in the registry; free float below the exchange minimum is a structural rather than a manipulation-class flag. *Related parties*: not disclosed in anything we could archive — stated as a gap. *Structure*: a 2024 IPO with an immediate change of control, a thin float, and a director resignation eleven months later [S6][S5] are optics-class items that deserve monitoring, not a pass. The one substantive accounting caveat is D&A: the pack shows depreciation of IDR5.9bn against gross PP&E of IDR409.9bn [S0], a ratio far below what a mine and plant of that size should carry, the classic direct-method understatement on IDX. We could not fetch the LK notes to restate it. EBITDA is unaffected because D&A is non-cash, but reported net profit and book value are overstated relative to a proper charge, which is why our valuation leans on the life DCF and not on PE or P/BV.

We value NICE on a life-of-mine DCF at the deck's through-cycle nickel price, with no terminal value — the method the house uses for depleting commodity assets and the one ANTM was just published on. The reason is not ideology: this company's earnings are a residual between an administered ore price and a mostly fixed cost base, so a multiple on any single year's EBITDA is a bet on where in the cycle that year sits. The method card's first rule is that a cyclical valued on spot or current-year earnings is a procyclical error; for an ore miner whose price is set monthly by decree, that error is unusually large.

The cost of capital is built bottom-up. The risk-free rate is 7.4% in US dollars, less the Indonesian default spread of 1.6% embedded in that dollar rate; we then add the industry unlevered beta 1.10 relevered to 1.24 at the company's market gearing times the equity risk premium of 4.2% plus the country risk premium of 2.5%. Written out, the cost of equity is 7.4% − 1.6% + 1.24 × (4.2% + 2.5%) = 14.1%, and degearing the same inputs at the 14.3% debt weight with an after-tax cost of debt of 9.4% pre-tax gives the WACC of 13.2%. We carry that rate rather than a lower one because the asset is single-mine, single-commodity, thinly traded and 10.4% free float; the spread over the risk-free rate is doing real work here, and a reader who prefers a lower rate should read the sensitivity table, where the value is shown against the nickel price and the rupiah.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR1,073.2bn; netting the balance-sheet debt gives the mechanical equity figure, and after the wind-down bridge described below the equity is worth Rp140 a share. The construction of the life is the part that matters and it has changed since initiation. The ore is now a reserve, not a forecast horizon: 25,000 kt of opening FY2025A ore reserve, which is ten years at the company's 2,500 kt plan and is delivered as nine years at the plan rate, a 2,000 kt taper year and a 500 kt residual year, seeded from the only reserve evidence in the record — Ditjen Minerba's statement that national nickel reserves, saprolite above all, support less than ten years of production without further exploration [S15] — and depleted year by year by the model. Because the reserve line caps volume, the final years are not a cliff; after the residual year there is no ore, no revenue, no terminal value and no growth input.

The life calculation stops one year early and we correct for it rather than hide it. The engine takes the best cumulative present value of the annual cash flows, and because the residual year and the payables unwind that follows it are outflows, that maximum is reached at the last full production year: the model computes the residual year's free cash flow of IDR-116.0bn and the following year's IDR-56.4bn, and both fall outside the sum the DCF uses. That is not a rounding matter — paying a mine's creditors at closure is a real cost, and leaving it out is what would flatter the value. We therefore carry the present value of those two years as a negative bridge item, shown line by line with its amount in the valuation table below, so that the equity value here is the full-life number and not the higher figure the mechanical stop would produce. We show the life sensitivity in the scenario table rather than asserting it: the bear cuts the reserve by thirty percent and ends the mine around FY2032E, the bull raises it by half and runs it well beyond the base horizon. There is no published company reserve to check either case against, and that absence is the single largest source of error in this valuation — doubling the life roughly doubles the DCF, which is why the stock is a call on a disclosure as much as on nickel.

The cross-checks disagree with the DCF in both directions, and the disagreement is informative rather than embarrassing. The EV/EBITDA method as the engine runs it applies the peer median to **last-twelve- month** EBITDA, which still carries the fourth-quarter charge, and so lands at a fraction of the DCF; run instead on the normalised FY2026E EBITDA of IDR242.2bn at the same peer-median multiple the cross-check lands **above** the DCF and close to the share price. That gap is the capex the multiple ignores: FY2026E capex is IDR212.5bn against EBITDA of IDR242.2bn [S0], and a multiple on EBITDA capitalises the mine before it pays for its own plant and before the reserve runs out. The P/BV cross-check applies a peer median to audited book equity of IDR147.9bn at the 31 March 2026 balance sheet — the only book figure we use; the forecast equity line rises with retained earnings and describes no balance sheet that exists yet — which is small only because the pre-IPO distributions in FY2022A-FY2023A went to the former owners [S0]; book is not an anchor for a mine whose depreciation charge is the one the pack shows. We therefore weight the DCF in full and show both multiples as cross-checks a reader can rebuild — but the reader should know that the honest range they bracket is wide, with the DCF at the bottom and the normalised multiple at the top, and that the share price sits between them. That is why the rating is HOLD rather than a directional call, and it is why the per-share value in the DCF is not the same number as the target.

Read the grid as the answer to "what is the mine worth at a different nickel price". At four fifths of the house deck the value is nil — the ore margin disappears before the fixed cost base does — and at six fifths it is well above the share price. Spot nickel sits a step below the deck's through-cycle marker, so the relevant column is the one immediately to the left of centre: there the value is well under the Rp234 share price, as the reverse DCF below also says, and still far above the zero at the trough. Read the grid for slope and sign rather than as a decomposition of the base: every cell re-runs the whole model under the override instead of scaling the base result, so the centre column does not reproduce the Rp159 twelve-month base value, and it is the shape — a cliff on the left, steep convexity to the right — that carries the information. The cost-curve position that the method card asks for cannot be sourced: no archived disclosure gives NICE's cash cost in a peer-comparable form, so we cannot place it in a quartile. What the model does say is that at a cash cost of 24 per wet tonne against an ore price of US$30.8 the margin is thin enough that a twenty percent fall in the ore price takes the value to zero. That is a fourth-quartile behaviour whatever the quartile actually is, and it is the honest answer to the card's moat question.

The largest sensitivity is not in the grid above: it is the ore grade. The HPM schedule steps from US$25.3/wmt in the limonite band to US$45.8/wmt one band up [S13][F5][F6]. A one-band upgrade in the grade NICE actually ships would raise revenue per tonne by roughly four fifths at unchanged costs and would move the target by more than any nickel-price scenario in this report. We have not put that in the base case because no archived source states the grade; a company disclosure of shipped grade is the first thing we would look for in the next results release.

What does the price imply? The reverse DCF solves for the nickel price that makes the DCF equal today's share price: 19,610, against the house deck's US$17,500 and the archived LME spot print of US$16,375 [S9][F7]. In other words the market is paying for a nickel price above both the through-cycle marker and spot, on a mine life nobody has published. That is a coherent thing to do if you believe the Indonesian enforcement story and a reserve upgrade; it is not what the published record supports today.

At the current price the shares trade on 8.3 times our FY2026E earnings, 6.4 times EV/EBITDA and 4.5 times book. The dividend yield is zero and stays zero in our forecast: the pack records no distribution after the 2024 listing, and the pre-IPO payouts went to the then-owners [S0]. For a commodity name whose market usually anchors on dividend capacity, the absence of a payout removes the floor IDX coal and nickel investors normally rely on, and it is a reason to require a wider discount to NAV rather than a reason to pay up for growth.

**Base case (probability 46.0%)** is the most probable path: ore volumes on the company plan at 2,500 kt, the ore price following the HPM at our calibrated realisation, costs held flat in real terms, and the reserve depleting to zero around FY2035E with nothing after. It produces EBITDA of IDR319.1bn at the plateau and a today's-value of Rp140.

**Bear case (12.0%)** mirrors the same four drivers downward: nickel at four fifths of the deck, volumes five percent lower, the ore realisation a further five percent weaker as smelters use their stockpile cover to press the HPM down [S13], and a reserve thirty percent smaller that ends the mine around FY2032E. This is the scenario in which the 2026-2027 quota is not cut, the LME/Shanghai surplus the regulator described [S8] keeps the metal price near the bottom of its range, and a thin-margin ore supplier meets it with IDR126.3bn of net debt. Its value is Rp0: at a nickel trough this asset is not cheap, it is worthless, and that convexity is the single most important number in the report.

**Bull case (42.0%)** is the enforcement and reserve story: nickel at six fifths of the deck as Indonesia's ore-trading crackdown bites [S9], volumes five percent higher on capacity the capex programme built, the realisation five percent better as the grade mix improves, and a reserve half again as large that runs the mine well past the base horizon. The probability is anchored on the commodity capex-turnaround base rate for this industry rather than on our judgement, and it is why the probability-weighted target sits above the DCF. The formula change by the ministry in April 2026, which raised the HPM precisely to capture a premium Indonesian ore was not getting [S14], is the mechanism by which a higher nickel price would reach NICE's realised price rather than being absorbed by the schedule.
Ranked downside risks, with likelihood × impact:

items: **Ore-price risk (high likelihood, high impact).** The HPM is set monthly by ESDM and the 2026 quota
came in above the original plan [S8][F8]. At this margin a fifth off the ore price takes the equity to
zero, which is the bear case and not a tail.
**Mine-life and licence risk (medium likelihood, high impact).** No company reserve or resource
statement is in the archived record and no IUP number or expiry could be archived either; the mine is
all of revenue, so a renewal condition, a licence dispute or a reclamation order is the one
non-market way to lose the whole equity. The base carries neither a renewal failure nor a quantified
reclamation obligation, and both are stated gaps rather than cleared.
**Balance-sheet and refinancing risk (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Gross debt of
IDR236.8bn against equity of IDR147.9bn, mostly short-dated bank
lines and working-capital facilities rather than bonds [S0].
**Grade risk (medium likelihood, high impact).** The HPM cliff between the grade bands means a
small change in the shipped grade is a large change in revenue per tonne [S13].
**Accounting risk (medium likelihood, medium impact).** An unidentified fourth-quarter charge and
inventory growth well ahead of cost of sales [S0]; if the charge is a cash obligation it comes off
equity directly and is not in our forecast.
**Governance and liquidity (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Free float of
10.4%, insider holdings of 89.6% and average daily turnover of
IDR1,294.6m [S0]; a controlling shareholder at that level can change the company's
shape without a minority vote that matters.
**Currency (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Revenue is dollar-linked through the HPM; costs are
part dollar, part rupiah. A stronger rupiah compresses the translated margin.
**Weather and operations (medium likelihood, low impact).** Laterite mining is rain-sensitive; the
industry press flagged drought and water constraints as a swing factor on smelter demand [S13].

blocks.text: The other side of the register is not in the probabilities and a reader should know why. ITMG paid Rp438 a share for 9.62% in July 2025 [S4][F9], which values the whole equity well above both the DCF and the current price, and the 10.4% float has to reach the exchange minimum by 2029 — a sell-down, a placement or a control transaction. We do not put that in the base because a private block trade at a premium is not an entitlement of a minority holder and the shares have since traded well below it; we treat it as the path by which the bull case would arrive, and it is the reason the bull carries close to a two-fifths weight rather than a tail.

Signposts that would change our view, in order of weight: a published JORC reserve or resource statement with a mine life beyond our window; a company disclosure of a shipped ore grade in a higher band; the 2027 RKAB coming in below the 2026 allocation [S8]; a return to positive free cash flow after the capex programme; and any move by LX International or ITMG to increase their stakes at a premium, which would put a strategic value on the asset that a DCF cannot see.

Ownership is concentrated and foreign-controlled. LX International Corp of Korea holds control through PT Energi Battery Indonesia, which it owns 99.99% [S6][F11]; insiders and affiliates hold 89.6% of the shares and institutions effectively none [S0]. ITMG's 9.62% stake was bought in the market at Rp438 in July 2025 [S4][F9][F10], a price that values the whole equity at roughly three times our DCF and nearly twice today's quote — an industrial buyer with diligence access paid up, and the market has since disagreed. That is either a stale transaction price in a thin float or a strategic value the DCF cannot see; we treat it as the latter for the bull case and not as a floor for minorities. Free float of 10.4% [S0] is below the exchange's minimum threshold; the registry's compliance deadline for a small issuer is 2029, so there is no immediate forced selling, but the stock is excluded from index eligibility and trades with a liquidity discount that we apply explicitly in the valuation. The float cure itself — a sell-down by LXI or a placement — is a downside risk to the price and an upside risk to liquidity, and it is the most likely route to a control event we can see.

The board is Korean-led with an independent commissioner chairing the audit committee [S5], a better structure than many IDX small caps. The governance items we would watch are the ones the record actually shows: an IPO in January 2024 immediately followed by a change of control [S6]; a director resignation in June 2025 announced with the standard assurance of no operational impact [S5]; and a fourth-quarter charge of that scale in FY2025 that turned a profitable year into a loss [S0] without, in anything we could archive, a clear explanation of what was impaired. A charge of that size at a company with IDR147.9bn of equity deserves an explanation in the notes; we could not fetch them.

On related parties our answer is honest and thin: nothing in the archived record we could retrieve quantifies sales to, purchases from or loans to affiliates of either controlling group [S4][S6]. For a company whose parent is a Korean trading house with an EV-materials strategy and whose second-largest holder is a coal group diversifying into nickel, related-party ore offtake is the modal risk on IDX and we have no evidence either way. This is flagged as an open item rather than cleared.

Dividends: none since listing, and none in our forecast [S0]. The pre-IPO distributions in FY2022A and FY2023A went to the then-owners, normal for an Indonesian listing but meaning there is no dividend record to judge policy against. Auditor and opinion: not in the archived record; the FY2025 accounts carry a large one-off and an understated depreciation charge, which are exactly the two things an audit opinion should be read for.

ESG exposures are the industry-standard ones for Indonesian nickel [S13]. Mine-site rehabilitation and post-closure obligations are unquantified in our record. Water and tailings management at a laterite operation are lower-risk than at a tailings-dam-intensive operation, but haul-road dust and river sedimentation are the local issues. The downstream chain matters for a Korean-controlled producer: Korean and European buyers of EV materials increasingly require provenance and carbon accounting, which is an opportunity for a company with a strategic parent and a compliance cost for one without. We found no enforcement action, HSC listing or index deletion against NICE in the registry, and we state that as a checked negative rather than an assumption.

The Indonesian exchange's minimum free-float rule tightened in 2026 as part of a broader move against
concentrated-ownership listings, and the market has been repricing companies whose controllers hold
nearly all the shares. For a small-cap miner the practical consequences are a wider bid-ask spread, no
index inclusion, and limited institutional participation — all of which feed into the discount rate
rather than into the operating forecast.
Dated catalysts:

items: **FY2026 results (from November 2026).** The first full year at the higher volume base. We want three
numbers: ore tonnes sold, revenue per wet tonne (which reveals the grade), and capex with the debt
balance [S0].
**ESDM 2027 nickel RKAB (first quarter 2027).** The ministry has said it will set the 2027 quota against
the LME and Shanghai surplus [S8]; a cut below the 2026 allocation is the bull case's trigger and a
repeat of the larger quota is the bear's.
**Monthly HPM decisions.** The government schedule for NICE's grade band is published twice monthly and
is the company's realised price [S13]; the step between the limonite and saprolite bands is the number to watch.
**Free-float compliance (by 2029).** A sub-threshold float for a small issuer has a deadline; any
placement or secondary sell-down by LX International or ITMG would change the liquidity discount and
the index status [S0].
**Any reserve or resource statement.** Not dated, but the highest-value disclosure the company could
make.

blocks.text: Between updates we monitor [S0][S13]: the monthly HPM for the ore bands we model; LME nickel and the Indonesian ore premium implied by the gap between the two; RKAB news flow; the company's quarterly debt and capex; ITMG's and LX International's disclosed holdings; and any change in free float. We would revisit the rating on a reserve statement, a grade disclosure in a higher band, or a material fall in the ore price that our realisation cannot absorb.

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: Ore sales in kt wmt. FY2023A actual was 2.01m wmt (F1/S2) and management guided 2.5m wmt for both 2025 and 2026 (F3/S2), with 1.8m wmt the 2024 target (F2/S2). The base case holds the company's own 2,500 kt plan flat: it is the only volume number the company has published for the forecast years, and FY2025A revenue of Rp1,177.7bn (S0) back-solves to between 2.5m and 2.7m wmt depending on the realised price, so 2,500 kt is neither above nor below the last actual on the plan price. The previously modelled 3,000-3,300 kt was an annualisation of one quarter and 32% above guidance; the capacity it assumed is not in any archived source, so it now sits in the bull case. Growth beyond the plan is not assumed anywhere in the base. Life comes from the reserve line (25,000 kt of opening FY2025A reserve, see params_basis), which depletes nine years at the 2,500 kt plan rate, then a 2,000 kt taper year and a 500 kt residual year; the engine caps volume at the remaining reserve so there is no cliff and no value after the ore is gone. Bear and bull shorten and lengthen the reserve rather than the plan rate.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the last actual, not on a forecast spike. FY2025A revenue of Rp1,177.7bn (S0) over about 2.67m wmt of ore is roughly US$27/wmt; against a 2025 LME nickel average near US$15,000/t that is a realisation of about 0.0018 of the metal price per tonne. The cross-check is the government ore price: the HPM for 1.2% Ni limonite was US$25.33/wmt in the second half of October 2026 (F5/S13) against an LME of US$16,375/t (F7/S9), a ratio of 0.00155, and the HPM for 1.35-1.4% material would be higher. NICE's ore is a laterite/limonite product sold into RKEF smelters, so the company's price is set by the HPM formula rather than by the metal price directly; 0.0018 is the ratio the actual revenue implies and it is held FLAT across the forecast — no unsourced discount and no unsourced premium. The 1.2-1.3% grade step in the HPM table (US$25.33 to US$45.83, F5-F6/S13) is the single biggest sensitivity in the model: a one-step upgrade in grade would roughly double revenue per wmt. The formula itself was re-set on 15 April 2026 by Kepmen ESDM 144/2026, which adjusted the nickel ore Corrective Factor, added iron, cobalt and chromium by-product credits to the calculation and moved the quotation from USD/DMT to USD/WMT (S14); the only HPM table we hold post-dates that decision (S13), and at 1.2% Ni it prices ore at a ratio of 0.00155 of LME, i.e. BELOW our calibrated 0.0018, so the re-set is already inside the ratio we use rather than a further unsourced uplift on top of it. The grade NICE ships is still undisclosed: an ore priced at the 1.2% band would be about 18% below our base price and one at the 1.3% band about 49% above it, which is why the band is the first thing to watch. Royalty is governed by PP 19/2025 and the proposed increase covering nickel was postponed in May 2026 (S16), so no rate rise is in the forecast.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: No domestic price cap applies to nickel ore; the HPM is a floor-setting reference, not a cap (S13).

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Used as the template's cost-intensity factor at 1.0, i.e. one tonne of ore moved and sold per tonne of ore sold; the mining cost per wmt then sits in cost_per_bcm. No archived source states NICE's overburden strip ratio (the annual report is not fetchable), so a bcm/tonne ratio would be a typed assumption. The company mines laterite from a shallow deposit at Lameruru (S3); a laterite profile of this type is mined at low stripping, and holding the intensity at 1.0 keeps the cost per tonne tied to the reported COGS rather than to an invented ratio.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: Mining cost per wmt in USD: US$12.0. Total cash cost is built to reproduce the FY2025A reported COGS of Rp914.1bn (S0) — about US$21/wmt including royalty and D&A — with mining at US$12, hauling, barging and port at US$5.5 (other_cost_unit) and royalty on top. Cost is held flat in nominal dollars and escalated only through the fuel link (d.coal.ici4, 30% of mining cost), which is the method card's nominal-consistent rule: no real-term cost deflation without a source. The FY2025 COGS is the right anchor because 2025 was the last full year at a settled ore price; FY2024's higher COGS per tonne reflects the lower volume against a largely fixed cost base.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Engine default 0.3 kept: no archived breakdown of NICE's mining cost into fuel and non-fuel. The fuel link still matters because ici4 is the industry's pinned fuel driver (operating configuration).

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: US$5.5/wmt for road haulage from the Lameruru pit to the coast, barging and port handling. The mine is inland but close to the coast and to Kendari (S3), which is why the non-mining cost is set below the mining cost; the combined US$17.5/wmt is the level needed to reproduce FY2025A COGS before royalty (S0). Held flat in USD.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Engine constant 0.135 of ore revenue, used as a placeholder rather than a view. The royalty regime in force is PP 19/2025, and the proposed increase that would have lifted nickel was postponed by the ESDM minister in May 2026 pending a new formula (S16), so no rate rise is modelled. The archived record does not carry the nickel-ore rate schedule itself — the LK notes are not fetchable (akp.co.id renders client-side) and no regulator page with the tariff was reachable — so this is the one input in the model with no source of its own. It is stated as such in §3 and §5 rather than described as conservative: a lower effective rate is upside risk that is not in the base, a higher one after the postponed revision is down risk, and the report gives the reader the EBITDA sensitivity to either. `royalty_selection` in the model records that the industry config has no IUP schedule for nickel, which is why the flat rate applies.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: Zero. The pack's non-operating income line is immaterial and the company describes 95% of revenue as nickel-ore sales (S10); the port and laboratory services in the profile are ancillary and not separately disclosed.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: No other revenue is modelled, so the margin is inert (engine default 0.1).

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: IDR per wmt, from the pack: FY2025A D&A of Rp5.86bn over 2.67m wmt is about Rp2,195/t, and PP&E nearly tripled to Rp409.9bn in FY2025 (S0), so FY2026E steps up to Rp3,800/t and then Rp4,500/t as the new plant depreciates. IMPORTANT EARLY-WARNING for the reader: the pack's D&A is only 1.4% of gross PP&E, far below a normal depreciation charge for a mine and plant of this size, which is the classic IDX direct-method understatement; the LK notes could not be fetched to restate it. If the true charge is 5-6x higher, EBITDA is unchanged (D&A is non-cash) but net profit and the P/B anchor are overstated here, which is why the valuation leans on the life DCF and EV/EBITDA, not on PE.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: IDR per wmt. FY2025A capex was Rp238.6bn on 2.67m wmt, about Rp89,400/t, and FY2024A Rp116.7bn (S0): the company has been building hauling, stockpile and port capacity while raising debt (gross debt Rp236.8bn at 2026Q1 from Rp133.8bn at FY2025, S0). FY2026E is held at Rp85,000/t to finish that programme, then capex falls to a maintenance level of Rp30,000/t from FY2028E. No itemised capex budget could be archived; the level is the reported run-rate, not a guess.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Zero separately; the expansion spend is carried inside capex_unit because the company does not disclose a project split. If the Rp100bn Shinhan facility drawn in 2026 (S0 debt path) funds a discrete project, that project's capex is already in the FY2026E unit rate.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: -15.9%, calibrated on the last actual: operating working capital was Rp186.9bn negative against revenue of Rp1,177.7bn in FY2025A (S0), the company funding itself on supplier credit, and current liabilities were Rp483.5bn against current assets of Rp174.2bn at the same date (S0). The engine default of -7.3% is the three-year average and it swings the other way: it assumes the ratio reverts to less supplier-funded working capital in FY2026E, which books a one-off cash outflow of roughly Rp90bn that neither the last actual nor the 2026Q1 balance sheet shows. Holding the last actual ratio is the method card's calibration rule and it keeps the cash line positive.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 22%, the Indonesian statutory corporate rate, instead of the engine's 35% average which is an artefact of FY2025's negative pre-tax profit (tax of Rp52.9bn on a loss, S0). A miner with a tax loss carry-forward pays little cash tax near term, so 22% is already the conservative end.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Engine default 9.74% (average of FY2023A-FY2025A interest over opening debt); consistent with the Rp100bn Shinhan facility drawn in 2026 and Indonesian rupiah corporate borrowing for a small miner.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Engine default 3.26% from the FY2023A-FY2025A history (S0).

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Rp103.0bn in FY2026E, then zero. Gross debt rose from Rp133.8bn at 31 December 2025 to Rp236.8bn at 31 March 2026 while capex ran ahead of operating cash flow (S0), and that drawdown is the only disclosed new borrowing in the record (the Rp100bn Shinhan facility). Carrying the FY2025 balance into the forecast without it would understate both interest and leverage against the balance sheet the market actually sees, so it is booked in FY2026E to arrive at the 2026Q1 gross debt; after that the assumption is that a company at three times reported EBITDA stops adding debt without a disclosed purpose.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero, but note that FY2025A carries a large one-off inside opex: Q4 2025 EBIT was a Rp158.9bn loss against Rp69.5bn of profit in Q3 on a similar revenue base (S0), i.e. roughly Rp179bn of impairment/one-off charges. It is excluded from the forecast by construction because it is not operating, and its existence is why FY2025A reported net profit is negative.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Nil; minority interest on the balance sheet is Rp0.35m (S0).

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero. The pack records no dividend after listing (dividends [], dps_ttm 0) and the pre-IPO distributions of FY2022A-FY2023A went to the then-owners (S0). Free float is 10.4% and the company is still funding capex from debt, so a payout would be a policy change with no evidence behind it.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue or placement in the record; 6,082.02m shares outstanding (S0).

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Zero. This is a depleting ore body with no reserve statement archived: the DCF runs to FY2035E and carries no terminal value, so growth after the horizon would be an asset that does not exist in the record. The engine's dcf_life weight and life_end logic then stops the discounting at the last year that adds value.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 5.5% of revenue. The engine default of 10.8% is polluted by FY2025's Rp226.5bn opex, which contains the ~Rp179bn Q4 one-off (S0). Excluding it, FY2025A opex was about Rp48bn on Rp1,177.7bn, or 4.1%; FY2023A was 5.3% and FY2024A 7.8% on a smaller revenue base. 5.5% is the normalised middle and is held flat.

challenges.challenge: The DCF stops at FY2035E in a year that still sells 2,500 kt for EBITDA of Rp406.5bn, then shows exactly zero in FY2036E with no wind-down, no closure cost and no residual asset value; no reserve or resource statement anywhere supports a ten-year life and the analyst concedes doubling the window doubles the DCF (177 to about 354, target about 404 vs the Rp234 price). This single uncited input is the difference between REDUCE and BUY.
challenges.answer: The life is now reserve-driven, not a forecast horizon. A reserve fact of 25,000 kt seeds the template's reserve line and the engine depletes it, capping volume at the remaining ore; the plan rate carries nine years, volume steps down and the final year is the residual tonnes. After that there is no revenue, no terminal value and no growth. The reserve is sourced to Ditjen Minerba's statement that national reserves support less than ten years of production; the bear cuts it 30% and the bull adds half, so the life sensitivity is in the scenario table. DCF moved 177 -> 148 and the target 207 -> 236, rating REDUCE -> HOLD.

challenges.challenge: The cross-check paragraph is wrong on its own arithmetic. Peer-median EV/EBITDA is 5.96x; on normalised FY2026E EBITDA of Rp290.6bn that is EV Rp1,732bn and equity Rp256 per share, 45% ABOVE the DCF 177 and above the Rp234 price - not several times the equity value. The fraction-of-the-DCF result comes only from applying the multiple to trailing EBITDA that includes the Rp179bn charge the analyst itself excludes. The 100% DCF weight and the unflagged weights.changed WARN rest on this misstatement.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt. The cross-check paragraph now states plainly that the engine's EV/EBITDA applies the peer median to LTM EBITDA carrying the Q4 charge and lands below the DCF, while the same multiple on normalised FY2026E EBITDA of 242.2 lands above the DCF and near the price; the gap is the 212.5 capex the multiple capitalises past. P/BV is shown as meaningless because the pre-IPO distributions left book at 147.9. The 100% DCF weight is retained but now justified in qc_justifications with the arithmetic, not with a discredited claim.

challenges.challenge: The rating is produced by the liquidity discount, not by the analysis: probability-weighted TP is Rp229.5 against a Rp234 price (-1.9%), and only the 10% house liquidity discount takes it to Rp206.6 (-11.7%). The investment summary says the target after the house liquidity discount is Rp207 without disclosing that 207 is 17% ABOVE the DCF 177, so a reader is told the REDUCE rests on a 177 value it does not rest on.
challenges.answer: The summary now shows the chain as three separate line items: DCF today 148, twelve-month roll-forward 169, probability-weighted 262, liquidity discount 10% giving the 236 target with +0.9% return. It states explicitly that the target is not the discounted DCF and that the rating says the market is roughly right, and the REDUCE-based sentence is gone.

challenges.challenge: S14 (detikFinance, 15 Apr 2026, Kepmen ESDM 144/2026) records that the nickel HPM formula was changed because ore prices were too low and a market premium was not captured in the HPM - a structural upward re-set of precisely the price NICE is paid. S14 is archived, cited nowhere, and realisation is held flat at the FY2026E level for ten years. The report premise that the price is administratively set by the HPM is contradicted by the same source.
challenges.answer: S14 is now cited in section 2 and in the bull case: Kepmen ESDM 144/2026 adjusted the nickel-ore Corrective Factor, added Fe/Co/Cr credits and moved to a wet-tonne quotation because ore prices were too low and a premium was not captured. The realisation is left at 0.0018 because the only post-change HPM table prices 1.2% ore at a ratio below ours, so the re-set is already inside the calibrated ratio and a further uplift would be unsourced; the grade-band upside is stated as the bull mechanism.

challenges.challenge: The register is treated only as a risk. ITMG paid Rp438 per share for 9.62% in July 2025 (S4/F10), 87% above the Rp234 price - an industrial buyer with diligence access valuing the equity at about Rp2,664bn against the DCF Rp1,079bn. LXI holds about 80% through EBI and the 10.38% float must reach 15% by 2029, which implies either a sell-down or placement that cures liquidity and index eligibility or a control transaction. None of this is in any scenario.
challenges.answer: The Rp438 block trade and the 10.38% float now appear in section 5 and section 6 with their arithmetic: the price values the whole equity at roughly three times our DCF and nearly twice the quote, the float must reach the exchange minimum by 2029, and the cure is either a sell-down or a control event. It is carried as the route by which the bull case arrives, and the bull probability is raised to 0.42 partly for it, but not as a minority entitlement in the base.

challenges.challenge: The Rp179bn Q4-2025 charge is excluded as non-operating with no source, in the same quarter current liabilities jumped Rp176.8bn (306.7 to 483.5) and inventory is not written down. If it is a provision, royalty or tax true-up rather than an impairment, it is a cash obligation: FY2026E FCFF of -94bn and the debt path are then understated. The earnings-quality section calls a -28% accruals ratio benign when OCF of 125.5bn sits on a 138.1bn working-capital release, and it reports that the pack has no receivables series when the pack has four years of them and inventory outgrew COGS 162% vs 78%.
challenges.answer: We could not identify the charge: the two archived announcement pages carry no item text. The report now says so, states that excluding it is a judgement not a sourced treatment, notes the concurrent jump in current liabilities, and flags that if it is a provision or tax true-up it is a cash obligation that comes off equity directly. The accruals, inventory and receivables tests are rerun on the pack's four years: inventory outgrew cost of sales, receivables did not outgrow revenue, and the accruals benefit is a working-capital release.

challenges.challenge: Base volume is 3,300 kt in FY2027-28E, 32% above the company own 2,500 kt guidance for 2025-2026 (F3/S2); FY2026E at 3,000 kt rests on annualising one quarter of revenue. Neither the second crusher nor any capacity figure appears in an archived source, and section 5 describes 3,300 kt as ore volumes on the company plan when it is 800 kt above the plan. The calibration gate is waived, so the optimism is never tested.
challenges.answer: Base volume is now the company's 2,500 kt plan, held flat, with the reserve stepping it down at the end. The 3,300 kt profile and the second crusher are removed from the base; the crusher is a bull-case volume assumption only, and section 5 no longer calls any volume above the plan 'the company plan'.

challenges.challenge: The balance-sheet risk paragraph is wrong on all three numbers. Net debt at the latest balance sheet (31 Mar 2026) is Rp174.2bn (236.8 debt less 62.6 cash), not 226.3, which is the FY2026E forecast; FY2025A net debt/EBITDA is 2.9x, which is 5.3x on the 226.3 figure the sentence uses; and 226.3 over FY2026E EBITDA of 290.6 is 0.78x, not above three times. The model own debt line is stale at 133.8 with cash at -92.5bn, which also contradicts the claim of no new borrowing. This paragraph is the stated reason for a zero dividend.
challenges.answer: Fixed at the source.
